description: Hand-written patterns for dataset v2 (author: project maintainer with an AI assistant, October 2026). New intents plus extra natural phrasings for the original 12. Merged with data/intents.json (v1 patterns) and CLINC150 rows by `python -m src.data_v2`. Deliberately varied: casual, short, long, lowercase, a few typos, durations. Emergency phrasings (chest pain, can't breathe) are left out on purpose; src/safety.py handles them before the model.

responses: For a mild stomach ache, try resting, sipping water, and eating small, bland meals (toast, rice, bananas). Avoid fatty, spicy food and alcohol for a day. See a doctor if the pain is severe, lasts more than a couple of days, or comes with fever, vomiting blood, or black stools.

Stomach aches often settle on their own. A warm compress, small sips of fluids, and bland food can help. Get medical care quickly if the pain is sudden and severe, is in the lower right of your belly, or your stomach is hard and tender.

Rest and stay hydrated, and skip heavy or greasy meals until you feel better. If it's heartburn, avoid lying down right after eating. Pain that keeps coming back or wakes you up at night is worth checking with a doctor.

responses: With nausea or vomiting, the main thing is to avoid dehydration: take small, frequent sips of water or an oral rehydration drink. Wait to eat until the vomiting stops, then start with bland food. See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down for a day, see blood, or have severe belly pain.

Rest, sip clear fluids slowly, and avoid strong smells and greasy food. Ginger or plain crackers help some people. Get medical help if vomiting lasts more than a day or two, or you notice signs of dehydration like very little urine, dizziness, or a dry mouth.
Nausea often passes on its own. Sit upright, get fresh air, and sip water. For children, older adults, or anyone who can't keep fluids down, contact a doctor sooner.

responses: Diarrhea usually clears up within a few days. Drink plenty of fluids, ideally an oral rehydration solution, and eat bland foods. Wash your hands often. See a doctor if it lasts more than 2 days (1 day for a child), if there's blood in it, or if you have a high fever or signs of dehydration.
Keep sipping fluids to replace what you're losing, and avoid alcohol, caffeine, and fatty foods for now. Rest helps. Get medical advice if it's severe, bloody, black, or comes with strong belly pain.

Most diarrhea is from a short-lived infection or something you ate. Stay hydrated and eat small, plain meals. Older adults, young children, and people with other health conditions should contact a doctor sooner.

responses: Most back pain gets better within a few weeks. Keep gently moving rather than resting in bed, use heat or a cold pack, and consider an over-the-counter pain reliever if it's safe for you. See a doctor if it's from a fall or injury, doesn't improve, or spreads down your leg.

Try gentle stretching, a warm shower or heat pad, and avoid heavy lifting for a few days. Good posture and breaks from sitting help. Get urgent care if back pain comes with numbness around your groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, weakness in your legs, or a fever.
Back strain is very common. Stay active within what's comfortable, and use heat or ice. If the pain is severe, keeps getting worse, or lasts more than a few weeks, see a doctor or physiotherapist.

responses: Body aches are often from a viral illness, overexertion, or poor sleep. Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and consider a warm bath or an over-the-counter pain reliever if it's safe for you. See a doctor if the aches are severe, last more than a few days, or come with a high fever or a rash.

Gentle stretching, rest, and staying hydrated can ease achy muscles. If you also have a fever, cough, or sore throat, it may be a cold or flu. Get checked if a joint is red, hot, and swollen, or if you have unexplained aches for weeks.
Sore muscles after exercise usually ease within a few days: keep moving gently and use heat. Aches with dark urine, severe weakness, or a stiff neck need medical attention.

responses: Earaches often come from a cold or a mild ear infection and many get better on their own within a few days. A warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever (if safe for you) can help. Don't put cotton buds in your ear. See a doctor if there's discharge, high fever, swelling behind the ear, or hearing loss.

For ear pain, rest, keep the ear dry, and try a warm cloth over it. If it started after swimming, it may be swimmer's ear, which may need drops from a doctor or pharmacist. Children with earaches and a fever should be checked.
Ear pain that lasts more than 2 to 3 days, is severe, or comes with fluid coming out of the ear should be checked by a doctor.

responses: A toothache usually needs a dentist to fix the cause. Until then, rinse with warm salt water, use an over-the-counter pain reliever if it's safe for you, and avoid very hot, cold, or sweet foods. Don't put aspirin directly on your gum.

Try a cold compress on your cheek and keep the area clean. Book a dentist appointment if the pain lasts more than a day or two. Get urgent care if your face or jaw is swelling, or you have a fever with the toothache.
Tooth sensitivity can improve with a toothpaste for sensitive teeth and a soft brush. Persistent or throbbing pain often means a cavity or infection that a dentist should look at.

responses: Dizziness often passes. Sit or lie down until it does, then get up slowly. Drink some water, as dehydration is a common cause, and avoid driving while dizzy. See a doctor if it keeps happening or comes with a bad headache, fainting, vision changes, or weakness.

If you feel lightheaded when standing, rise slowly and keep well hydrated. A spinning feeling (vertigo) can come from the inner ear. Get emergency help if dizziness comes with slurred speech, a drooping face, numbness, or chest pain.
Rest somewhere safe until the dizziness eases, and have a snack if you haven't eaten. Repeated dizzy spells are worth discussing with a doctor, especially if you take blood pressure medicine.

responses: Tiredness is very common and often linked to sleep, stress, diet, or a recent illness. Try a regular sleep schedule, regular meals, staying hydrated, and some daily activity. If you've felt tired for more than a few weeks without a clear reason, see a doctor, who may check things like iron or thyroid levels.

Rest when you need to, but gentle activity and daylight can actually boost energy. Limit caffeine and alcohol. See a doctor if the fatigue comes with weight loss, fever, shortness of breath, or low mood that won't lift.
Feeling run down after a cold or flu can last a week or two. If it goes on longer, or you're struggling with daily tasks, it's worth a check-up.

responses: For trouble sleeping, keep a regular bedtime and wake time, avoid caffeine after midday, and put screens away an hour before bed. A cool, dark, quiet bedroom helps. If you can't fall asleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.

Stress often keeps people awake. Try a wind-down routine, like reading, a warm shower, or slow breathing. Avoid long daytime naps and heavy meals late at night. If poor sleep lasts for weeks or affects your daytime life, talk to a doctor.

Alcohol can make sleep worse later in the night. Daylight and exercise during the day help set your body clock. Ongoing insomnia is very treatable, and a doctor can suggest approaches like CBT for insomnia.

responses: For hay fever or mild allergies, an over-the-counter antihistamine often helps, and saline rinses or eye drops can ease symptoms. Keep windows closed on high-pollen days and shower after being outdoors. A pharmacist can help you pick a suitable product.

Try to avoid your trigger where possible, whether pollen, dust, or pets. Washing bedding in hot water and using a damp cloth for dusting reduce dust mites. See a doctor if allergies affect your sleep or daily life, or if you also wheeze.
Mild allergy symptoms are usually manageable at home. Get emergency help right away if you have swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing after contact with an allergen.

responses: Many rashes settle on their own. Keep the skin cool and moisturized, avoid scratching, and stop using any new soap, cream, or detergent that might have caused it. An over-the-counter antihistamine or hydrocortisone cream may help itching. See a doctor if the rash spreads quickly, blisters, or you feel unwell.

For itchy skin, use fragrance-free moisturizer, lukewarm (not hot) showers, and loose cotton clothing. Get urgent care if a rash comes with fever, or if it doesn't fade when you press a glass against it.
Hives often come and go within a day. Note any new food, medicine, or product. Get emergency help if hives come with swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
